subpages.text_content: How to Choose a Paintless Dent Repair Technician | Dent Repair USA | Dent Repair USA | Service areas | 863-205-1582 | A guide from the bench | How to choose a paintless dent repair technician | Written by someone who has been doing this since 1999 and who would rather you asked hard questions — including of him. Most of what follows will help you judge any technician, not just this one. | The short answer | If you only do one thing, do this: send photos and ask whether paintless repair is even the right answer. The technician who tells you when it is not is the one worth hiring, because that answer costs him the job. Everything below is detail underneath that one test. | 1. Check the paint, not the dent | Paintless only works while the paint is unbroken. Cracked, chipped or scraped to primer means body shop. A good tech says so in the first minute. | 2. Ask what the guarantee covers | Ask for the amount and the duration, and who honours it if the person moves on. "Guaranteed" on its own is a word, not a promise. | 3. Get it in writing before anyone starts | A written estimate, panel by panel, with a time. Verbal numbers move. Written ones do not. | 4. For hail, ask who writes the estimate | It has to be one your adjuster will accept. Ask what estimating system they write in before you hand the car over. | What the certifications actually mean | Certification in this trade is worth asking about and worth keeping in proportion. For insurance and hail work, Vale certification carries weight because it is the estimating language claims get written in — an adjuster reading a Vale-format estimate is reading something familiar. Other industry and manufacturer certifications exist and are fair game to ask about. | But hold any certificate at its true value. It proves someone sat the training. It does not prove they are still sharp, still working, or honest about the jobs they should turn down. Ask who issued it, what it covers, and when. Then judge the answers to the questions below, which tell you far more. | The five questions worth asking | "Will you tell me if paintless is the wrong answer?" | The single best question. A yes costs him work. Listen for whether he has ever said no, and to what. | "Is the paint broken on this?" | This decides paintless versus body shop before anything else. He should be able to answer from a decent photo. | "What is the guarantee, and for how much?" | A number and a term. Ask what happens if the panel needs a second look in six months. | "Will my adjuster accept your estimate?" | Hail only. If the answer is vague, your claim is the thing that suffers. | "How do you price this?" | Per dent, per panel, per hour — any of them can be fair. Not being able to explain it is the problem. | What should decide the price | There is no flat rate, and a firm quote given over the phone without seeing the damage is a guess dressed as a number. Four things move the price: the size of the dent, where it sits on the panel, how hard the back of that panel is to reach, and how many there are. A door ding in the open middle of a panel is the cheap end. A crease along a bodyline, an aluminium panel, or a dent sitting behind a brace costs more, because it takes longer and carries more risk of going wrong. | Cheapest is not the win here. A dent pushed too far or too fast can stretch the metal, and stretched metal does not go back. Ask what happens if the repair does not come out perfect — the answer tells you whether you are buying a repair or a gamble. | Red flags — especially after a hailstorm | Offering to cover your deductible | Hard stop. In Florida this is treated as insurance fraud, and it is your claim and your name carrying the risk — not theirs. | A price before anyone has seen the car | Nobody can price hail from a phone call. A number that early is either a hook or a fiction. | Sign here first, estimate later | Never sign a blank authorisation or an open-ended contract before a written estimate is in your hand. | "We can fix anything" | Nobody can. Broken paint, chrome, glass and collision damage are all outside paintless repair. Someone who never says no has not told you the truth yet. | No local address, no local history | Storm crews arrive and leave. Ask who honours the guarantee in six months, and where they will be. | Cash only, no paperwork | No written estimate and no invoice means no guarantee you can hold anyone to. | Mobile or shop? | For everyday dents it genuinely does not matter — the work is identical, and mobile just means it happens where your car already is. Hail is the exception. Counting hail damage properly takes controlled light; an estimate written in a bright driveway will miss dents that a shop reading catches, and the ones missed are the ones you argue about with an adjuster later. If someone offers to assess a full hail car in your driveway, that is a shortcut you pay for at claim time. | Common questions | How do I know if a dent can be fixed without painting? | Look at the paint, not the dent. Paintless dent repair reshapes the original metal from behind, so it only works while the paint is unbroken. If the paint is cracked, chipped, flaked or scraped down to primer, the panel needs a body shop. A sharp crease on a bodyline can also be beyond it. A technician who looks at a photo and says "that one is not mine" is showing you the most useful thing about him. | What certifications should a paintless dent repair technician have? | For insurance and hail work, Vale certification is the one that carries weight with adjusters, because it is the estimating language claims are written in. Other manufacturer and industry certifications exist and are worth asking about. But treat any certificate as a floor, not a ceiling: ask who issued it, what it covers, and how long ago. A certificate proves training. It does not prove the person is still good, still working, or honest about what they cannot do. | What questions should I ask before hiring a dent repair technician? | Five that actually separate people: Will you tell me if paintless is the wrong answer? Is the paint broken on this damage? Do you carry a workmanship guarantee, for how much, and for how long? If this is a hail claim, will you write an estimate my adjuster will accept? And how do you price — per dent, per panel, or per hour? Anyone who answers all five plainly is worth your time. | How much should paintless dent repair cost? | There is no flat rate, and anyone quoting one over the phone without seeing the damage is guessing. Price follows four things: how big the dent is, where it sits on the panel, how hard the back of that panel is to reach, and how many dents there are. A door ding on an open panel is the cheap end. A crease on a bodyline, an aluminium panel, or a dent behind a brace costs more because it takes longer and risks more. | Is a mobile technician as good as a shop? | For everyday dents, yes — the work is the same and it happens where your car already is. Hail is the exception. Counting hail damage properly needs controlled light, and an estimate written in a driveway will miss dents that a shop reading will catch. If someone offers to assess a whole hail car in your driveway, that is a shortcut you will pay for at claim time. | Someone knocked on my door after a hailstorm. Should I use them? | Be careful. After a storm, crews travel in and leave again. Ask where they will be in six months if a panel needs a second look, and who honours the guarantee then. Two hard stops: nobody should offer to "cover" or "eat" your insurance deductible — in Florida that is treated as insurance fraud and it is your claim carrying the risk — and nobody should ask you to sign a blank authorisation or an open contract before you have a written estimate in hand. | Does paintless dent repair hurt my car's value? | The opposite, done right. Filler and fresh paint show up on a resale inspection and on the car's history. Reshaping the original metal leaves the factory finish in place, which is exactly what a buyer, a lease inspector, or an appraiser is looking for. | And if you want to hold us to it | Everything above is how we would want to be judged. subpages.meta_description: What actually decides the price of a dent: size, location on the panel, what is behind it, and how many there are. Why phone quotes are guesses, when paintless is cheaper than a body shop, and when to skip the insurance claim.
subpages.text_content: How Much Does Dent Repair Cost? A Technician Explains | Dent Repair USA | Dent Repair USA | Service areas | 863-205-1582 | A guide from the bench | How much does dent repair cost? | The honest answer is that four things decide it, and all four have to be seen. Here is what they are, so you can look at your own car and know roughly where you stand before anyone quotes you. | Published September 8, 2026 · Paul Whitehorn · Vale Certified Master Craftsman II | Send a photo, get a real number | The four things that set the price | There is no flat rate for a dent, and there cannot be one. Two dents the same width can differ several times over in price, and it is never arbitrary — it is these four, every time. | 1. How big it is | Depth matters more than width. A wide, shallow dish comes out faster than a small, deep one that has pushed the metal further out of shape. | 2. Where it sits | The open middle of a panel is the cheap spot. A bodyline, a panel edge, or the crown of a curve is stiffer metal and slower, more careful work. | 3. What is behind it | The repair happens from the back. Open access is quick. A brace, a foam block, a wiring loom or a sealed cavity means removing trim to reach it — or reaching it a much harder way. | 4. How many there are | Additional dents on the same panel cost far less each, because the expensive part — getting to the back of that panel — is already done. | Which is why nobody can price your dent on the phone. Not one of those four can be heard. A firm number given down a phone line is either a guess that will move when the technician sees the car, or a low hook to get someone into your driveway. Photographs answer all four in about thirty seconds — take one straight on and one at a low angle with light reflecting across the panel, and a real number can come back the same day. | Where your dent probably sits | These are real repairs, ordered from least expensive to most. Find the one that looks like yours and you will know which end of the range you are at. | Least expensive | The parking-lot door ding | Small, round, in the open middle of a door, paint unbroken. This is the benchmark every other repair is priced against — quick to reach, quick to work, and usually done while you wait. | If you have three of these across the car, ask for all three together. The second and third are much cheaper than the first. | Mid range | A crease, or a dent on a bodyline | A crease is stretched metal, and stretched metal does not come back in one push — it comes back in stages, working along the length of it. A dent sitting on a bodyline is the same problem, because that fold is the stiffest metal on the panel. | Same width as a door ding, several times the work. This is the most common place people are surprised by a price, and it is worth understanding rather than arguing about. | Mid range | A large dent with awkward access | Big is not automatically expensive — a large, shallow dent on an open panel can be straightforward. What adds cost is the panel it landed on. Decklids, roofs and quarter panels often mean removing trim, headliners or interior panels just to reach the back of the metal. | Ask specifically whether trim removal is in the price. It should be, and it should be said out loud. | Most expensive | Aluminium, or a sealed panel | Aluminium has no memory the way steel does. It will not spring back on its own, it work-hardens as you move it, and it usually needs heat and a much slower hand. Many technicians will not touch it. The panels that are glued or sealed shut are the same story for a different reason — the back of the metal is simply not reachable without significant disassembly. | These are still frequently worth doing, because the body shop alternative on an aluminium panel is not cheap either. | Judgement call | Extreme damage that is still paintless | Damage this severe can often still be done without paint, and when it can, it beats a body shop on both cost and on what it leaves behind — the original finish. But it is hours of work, and it is the category where an honest technician is most likely to tell you the answer is a body shop instead. | If someone looks at damage like this and promises perfection without hesitating, be more careful, not less. | Paintless versus a body shop | When the damage qualifies, paintless repair is substantially cheaper — and the reason is simply that it skips most of the job. A body shop repair means filling, sanding, priming, painting, then blending the new paint into the neighbouring panels so the colour matches, plus the days of shop time all of that takes. Paintless reshapes the metal that is already there. No filler, no paint, no blending, usually hours rather than days. | The qualifying condition is the paint. Paintless repair works while the finish is unbroken. Once the paint is cracked, chipped or scraped down to primer, no amount of metalwork fixes it, and the body shop is genuinely the right answer — not an upsell. A technician who tells you that is doing you the favour, because he has just talked himself out of the job. | There is a second, quieter saving. Filler and fresh paint show up on a resale inspection and can land in the car's history. The factory finish never being disturbed is worth real money later, which is why lease returns and trade-ins are two of the most common reasons people finally get a ding fixed. | Should you claim it on insurance? | For a single dent, usually not — and this is the part where getting the estimate first genuinely saves you money. Most single-dent repairs come in below a typical deductible. Filing in that case pays you nothing and still puts a claim on your record. | The order that works: get a written number first, then compare it to your deductible, then decide. Well above it, claim. Near or below it, pay outright and keep the claim. Any technician should hand you that number without a claim attached to it — and if the damage is hail rather than a single ding, the arithmetic changes completely, which is covered in the | hail claim guide | . | How to get a number you can trust | Send photographs, not descriptions. One straight on, one at a low angle with light reflecting across the panel so the shape of the dent shows. | Mention every dent , not just the one that bothers you. Grouping them is cheaper, and finding the others later is how estimates change. | Say whether the paint is broken. Run a fingernail across it — if it catches, say so. It decides the whole answer. | Ask for it in writing. Verbal numbers move. Written ones do not. | Ask what happens if it does not come out perfect. The answer tells you whether you are buying a repair or a gamble. | The longer version of that last point — how to judge the person, not just the price — is here: | how to choose a paintless dent repair technician | . | Common questions | How much does it cost to fix a door ding? | A single door ding in the open middle of a panel, with the paint unbroken, is the least expensive repair in this trade — it is the benchmark everything else is priced against. What moves it up is size, a position on a bodyline or panel edge, bracing or foam behind the panel, or a second and third dent. Any technician should give you a firm written number from clear photographs, free and without commitment. | Why won't anyone quote over the phone? | Because the four things that set the price cannot be heard. Size, exactly where on the panel it sits, what is behind that spot, and how many there are all have to be seen. A phone number is either a guess that will change on arrival, or a low hook to get into your driveway. Send photographs — a good photo answers all four in about thirty seconds. | Is paintless cheaper than a body shop? | Substantially, when the damage qualifies. A body shop repair means filling, sanding, priming, painting and blending into surrounding panels, plus days of shop time. Paintless reshapes the original metal from behind — no filler, no paint, no blending, usually hours instead of days. It only works while the paint is unbroken; once it is cracked or scraped to primer, the body shop is the correct answer. | Why does one dent cost more than another the same size? | Access and shape. A dent in the open middle of a door can be reached from behind and worked in minutes. The same dent on a bodyline, a panel edge, or over a brace, foam block, wiring loom or sealed cavity can take hours. Sharp creases also cost more than round dents, because stretched metal has to be brought back in stages rather than pushed out once. | Do multiple dents cost more each? | Less each, not more. Most of the cost of a single dent is setup — reaching the back of the panel, removing trim, setting the lights. Once a technician is inside a panel, additional dents on it are far cheaper than the first. One dent on four panels costs more than four dents on one panel, which is why it is worth mentioning all of them. | Should I claim it on insurance? | Get the written estimate first. Most single-dent repairs come in below a typical deductible, which means a claim would pay you nothing and still be a claim on your record. Well above your deductible, claiming makes sense. Near or below, pay outright. You should be able to get that number without a claim attached. | Can a dent be too small to fix? | Too small is rarely the problem — small shallow dings are among the most satisfying repairs. The honest limit is at the other end: metal stretched by a sharp impact, a crease running through a bodyline, or paint that has already cracked. A technician who tells you it is not worth doing, or not his job at all, is giving you the most valuable answer available. | Does it hurt my resale value? | Repairing it properly protects the value; leaving it does not. Filler and fresh paint show on a resale inspection and can appear in the vehicle history. Paintless repair leaves the factory finish untouched — exactly what a buyer, a lease-return inspector or an appraiser wants. That is the whole trade. | The name is the job description. We push dented metal back where it belongs and leave the factory paint exactly as the factory left it. If a repair needs paint, filler, a buffer or a new part, it is not our work — and saying so is the most useful thing we can tell you. | Published September 18, 2026 · Paul Whitehorn · Vale Certified Master Craftsman II | Send a photo, get a straight answer | What paintless actually means | A dent is metal that moved. Paintless dent repair reaches the back of that metal and moves it back — with hand tools, in stages, reading the reflection of a light across the panel. Nothing is filled, nothing is sanded, nothing is sprayed. When it is done, the paint on that panel is the paint the car was built with. | That single condition is what the whole trade rests on: the finish has to still be intact. Paintless repair works underneath the paint, so the paint has to be there to work under. Once it is cracked, chipped, scraped to primer or gone, no amount of metalwork brings it back, and a body shop is genuinely the right answer — not an upsell. | Ten-second test you can do yourself. Run a fingernail lightly across the damage. If your nail catches in it, the paint is broken — that is paint work, and not us. If the surface is smooth and the metal underneath is pushed in, that is a dent, and that is exactly us. | What we do | All of it is the same job wearing different clothes: metal moved back, finish untouched. | Door dings and parking-lot dents | The everyday one. Small, round, paint unbroken, usually done while you wait. | Hail damage, whole vehicles | Dozens or hundreds of dents, insurance work included. This is what paintless repair was built for. | Creases and bodyline dents | Stretched metal and stiff folds. Slower, staged work, still no paint. | Large dents with awkward access | Decklids, roofs, quarter panels — including removing trim to reach the back of the panel. | Lease returns and pre-sale | Dents out with the original finish intact, which is what an inspector and a buyer both want to see. | Dealership and wholesale work | Front-line units and auction cars, priced by the sheet, done on site at the dealership. | What we don't do — and these are not maybes | Every one of these is a real trade with its own tools, its own licence and its own expertise. We are not good at them, we are not equipped for them, and we are not going to pretend otherwise to keep a job in the building. | Never | Painting, of any kind | No panels, no spot repairs, no blending, no aerosol, no touch-up pen, no wheel paint, no bumper refinishing. Not a little bit as a favour. We do not own a spray gun and we do not want one — the entire point of what we do is that the factory finish is never disturbed. | Who to call: a body shop or a refinish shop. | Never | Body work | No filler, no sanding, no pulling collision damage, no welding, no panel replacement, no frame or structural work, no cracked plastic bumpers, no rust repair. If metal has been torn, stretched past saving, or needs to come off the car, that is a different trade. | Who to call: a collision or body shop. | Never | Glass | No windshields, no chip or crack repair, no back glass, no side windows, no sunroofs, no mirrors. We also do not calibrate the cameras and sensors that live behind a windshield. | Who to call: an auto glass company. | Never | Detailing and paint correction | No buffing, no polishing, no wet sanding, no compounding, no ceramic coating, no wraps or vinyl, no headlight restoration, no interior work, no washing. A car goes home from us with its dents gone, not with a new shine. | Who to call: a detailer or paint-correction specialist. | Never | Metal bumpers, wheels, mechanical and everything else | No chrome or steel bumper straightening, no wheel or rim repair, no suspension, alignment, mechanical or electrical work, no upholstery, no key cutting, no lockouts, no towing. | Who to call: the specialist for that part — and if you are not sure who, ask us and we will point you at one. | Scratches: the one honest maybe | This is the question that comes up most, so here is the whole truth about it. | A light mark that sits on top of the clear coat — no nail catch, nothing down to primer — can sometimes be improved or removed as part of a paintless repair, on the panel we are already working. Sometimes. It depends on the paint, the depth and what the metal underneath is doing, and the only way to know is to look at it in person under shop light. | Anything deeper than that is paint damage , and paint damage is a body shop's job. Keyed panels, scrapes from a wall or another car, sanded-through clear, primer or bare metal showing: none of that is repairable without paint, by anyone, and we would be lying to take the money. | And it is not a mobile visit. Scratch questions are judgement calls that need proper lighting and a fixed bench, so they happen at the shop in Lakeland — never in a driveway or a parking lot. Mobile visits are for dent repairs that have already been seen and priced. Honestly, it is not really what we do at all; if a scratch is the only thing wrong with the car, a body shop or a detailer will serve you better than we will. | Why we say no so plainly | A shop that says yes to everything is telling you it is expert at nothing. Twenty-six years in one trade is why the repairs come out right — and the price of that focus is a short list of things we will not touch. | There is also a plainer reason. If we sprayed a panel, filled a crease or buffed a scratch, you would no longer have an original-paint car. That is the one thing we are actually selling: a repair that leaves nothing behind for a resale inspection to find, no filler, no overspray, nothing in the vehicle history. Protecting that is worth turning work away for. | So when the answer is no, it will come with the name of the right trade for the job. That is not us dodging the work — it is the most valuable half of the estimate. | Straight answers to the usual questions | Do you paint? | No. Not a panel, not a spot, not a touch-up pen. Paintless repair works under the original finish — the moment paint is needed, the job belongs to a body shop. | Can you just buff that out? | Buffing is detailing, and we are not detailers. A mark on top of the clear coat may improve while we repair a dent on that panel; that is the whole extent of it. | My car got keyed. Can you help? | Not with the paint, which is the actual damage. That is a body shop. If the panel is also dented, we can take the dent out — the line will still need paint. | Can you fix my cracked bumper? | No. Cracked plastic needs plastic repair and refinishing. A dented metal bumper is not paintless work either — that is a bumper shop or a replacement. | Do you do windshield chips? | No glass work of any kind. A glass company will do it cheaper and better than anyone pretending to. | Can you repair rust, or a hole? | No. Once metal is corroded or pierced, there is nothing left to reshape. That is body shop territory. | Will you come to me for a scratch? | No — anything scratch-related is looked at in the shop, under shop light.
